For $\mathcal X\subset\mathbb R^d$, query $q$ and selected IVF lists $\mathcal L(q)$, the valid-pool pipeline is
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 q'&=\Pi q,&
 U(q)&=\bigcup_{\ell\in\mathcal L(q)}\mathrm{list}_\ell,\\
 c&=\max\{k,\lceil\alpha k\rceil\},&
 C_\alpha(q)&=\operatorname{Top}^{\rm P}_{\min(c,|U(q)|)}U(q),\\
 &&\mathcal R_\alpha(q)&=\operatorname{Top}^{\rm H}_k C_\alpha(q).
 \end{aligned}
\]
Top selection uses each computed score and its tie rule. The refined score includes a query-only constant (\cref{sec:2-3}); GT measures raw-neighbour recovery.

GPU construction, layout and search retain JHQ's square rotation and Cartesian primary/residual codes. One unlabelled-agreement multiplier is reused on a stable workload; it is neither per-query learning nor an absolute-recall certificate.

E1 tests squared-L2 top-10 on one RTX 5090, four datasets and batch 1,000. Six datasets support component/budget tests; T5 adds batches 8/32 (\cref{sec:7-smallbatch}). Search stays GPU-resident with host preparation/transfers. Updates, host paging, multi-GPU and billion-scale search are untested.
changes.after:
Given a vector database $\mathcal X\subset\mathbb R^d$ and query $q$,
the task is to return $k$ approximate nearest neighbours under squared
Euclidean distance. The research problem is to construct and search
JHQ's compressed index within a single GPU's memory, and improve query
throughput at a given recall target.

Search first selects relevant IVF lists, screens their vectors using
primary codes, then uses residual codes to rescore a smaller shortlist.
The refinement budget controls how many candidates enter this last stage.
Ground truth (GT) gives exact neighbours in the original vector space;
recall is the fraction of these neighbours recovered.

The study retains JHQ's dimension-preserving orthogonal transform and
hierarchical codes (\cref{sec:2-3}), and investigates GPU construction,
data layout, search execution and refinement-budget selection.
Calibration compares smaller-budget outputs with a larger-budget
reference without GT, then reuses one chosen multiplier for a fixed
index and an assumed stable query distribution. GT evaluation checks
the resulting recall.

Evaluation uses one RTX 5090 and squared-L2 top-10. The main cross-system
comparison uses four datasets and batch 1,000; lookup-table, memory-layout
and budget tests cover six datasets. A small-batch study adds batches
8/32 (\cref{sec:7-smallbatch}). The index and core search computation
remain on the GPU; preparing and transferring queries within the search
call are included in its timing. Dynamic updates, host paging and
multi-GPU execution are outside the implementation; billion-scale
search is not evaluated.

they share a corpus source. Alignment checks are reported in
\cref{sec:7-precision,sec:7-2}. BGE uses Italian Wikipedia, and Stella uses
the TREC24 BioGen corpus \cite{data_bge,data_stella}. The sizes below
describe the prepared exports.

OpenAI/BGE/Stella preparation removes vectors containing NaN or infinite
values (non-finite rows) and normalises nonzero vectors:
\[
 x\leftarrow x/\|x\|\quad(\|x\|>10^{-12}).
\]
Preparation scripts sample query rows without replacement using seed 42
and remove those rows from the base set. Stella retains 999 such corpus
queries, rather than the upstream 65-query set. This evaluates vector
neighbours of held-out corpus embeddings rather than relevance-labelled
user queries.

All methods use the same exported query and GT files. Preparation code
provides exhaustive squared-L2 GT over FP32 vectors through Faiss FlatL2
or a memory-bounded tiled scan. For query set $\mathcal Q$, returned ID
sets $\mathcal R_k(q)$ and stored GT prefixes $\mathcal T_k(q)$, recall is
\begin{equation}
\Recall@k=\frac{1}{|\mathcal Q|k}
\sum_{q\in\mathcal Q}|\mathcal R_k(q)\cap\mathcal T_k(q)|.
\label{eq:3-recall}
\end{equation}
GT files contain 100 neighbours for Vogue/arXiv and 20 for the others;
only the first ten count. Equal-distance alternatives outside that prefix
receive no automatic credit, and duplicate returned IDs add no hits.

JHQ uses $M=d/8$, $B=B_r=8$, eight coarse-training iterations and
100,000 database rows for residual training. Cached runs reuse models
but re-encode the database; cold runs refit them.
Budget calibration in Chapter 6 uses even-indexed query rows and evaluates
recall on odd-indexed rows, with zero-based indices:
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathcal Q_{\rm cal}&=\{q_i:i\bmod2=0\},&
 \mathcal Q_{\rm hold}&=\{q_i:i\bmod2=1\},\\
 (|\mathcal Q_{\rm cal}|,|\mathcal Q_{\rm hold}|)
 &=\begin{cases}(500,499),&\text{Stella},\\(500,500),&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}
 \end{aligned}
 \]
The budget harness uses seed 12345 to draw 64 subsets at each sample size
$S\in\{32,64,128\}$; FULL uses all 500 calibration queries. GT evaluates
quality and the diagnostic oracle, while agreement uses search outputs
(\cref{sec:6-2,sec:a-budget-contract}). These disjoint rows and repeated
subsets form a finite-pool experiment; population assumptions are analysed
in Chapter 6.

GPU search can parallelise across queries, candidates and coordinates.
Warps have 32 threads with bounded block resources \cite{cuda_programming_guide}.
JHQ's broad primary scan and narrower residual refinement expose
different amounts of work. More blocks can improve utilisation for small
query batches, but duplicate tables, local state and merging add work.
Scheduling must account for both available parallelism and this overhead.

Faiss uses warp selection \cite{johnson_gpu}; bitonic/radix/merge choices trade state for work, alongside global selectors AIR/GridSelect \cite{gpu_topk}.
changes.after:
GPU work is organised into thread blocks; threads within a block can
cooperate through shared memory. A warp is a group of 32 threads scheduled
together. Registers, shared memory and limits on resident blocks constrain
how much work can run concurrently \cite{cuda_programming_guide}.
Within this hierarchy, threads can process separate queries, score
different candidates for the same query, or share the coordinate
calculations for one candidate.

Candidate selection keeps the smallest scores from the scanned pool.
Faiss uses warp-level selection \cite{johnson_gpu}; other GPU top-$k$
methods distribute selection over larger arrays \cite{gpu_topk}.
Chapter 5 explains the selection and scheduling used by JHQ-GPU.

\subsection{What is inherited}

JHQ uses square $\Pi\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ \cite{jhq}:
\begin{equation}
 \begin{aligned}
 \Pi^\top\Pi=I
 &\Longrightarrow
 \|\Pi(q-x)\|^2\\
 &=(q-x)^\top\Pi^\top\Pi(q-x)=\|q-x\|^2.
 \end{aligned}
 \label{eq:2-isometry}
\end{equation}
Dimension stays $d$. Finite-precision geometry, GEMMs and quantisation are checked separately.

Partition $y$ into $M$ subspaces of dimension $D_s=d/M$. With $B$ bits per
primary subspace, $K=2^B$ labels are formed from $L=2^{B/D_s}$ scalar levels,
requiring the implemented Cartesian parameters to make $L$ an integer.
Writing $\Phi$ for the standard normal CDF, the constructor uses
\begin{equation}
 a_i=\sigma\Phi^{-1}\!\left(\frac{i-1/2}{L}\right),\quad
 i=1,\ldots,L,\qquad
 \mathcal C_m=\{a_1,\ldots,a_L\}^{D_s}.
 \label{eq:2-cartesian}
\end{equation}
At the evaluated $B=D_s=8$, $L=2$ and $\mathcal C_m=\{-a,+a\}^8$,
with $a\simeq0.67449\sigma$. Each byte records eight coordinate signs.
The implementation estimates $\sigma$ from vector energy; unit-normalised
inputs motivate the scale $1/\sqrt d$. This representation is prior art,
not an invention of the GPU execution layer.

Residuals are $r=y-\widehat p$, giving reconstruction $\widehat y=\widehat p+\widehat r$. The evaluated codes use $d/8$ primary bytes and $d$ residual bytes per vector, before metadata. Refining fewer rows reduces reads, not stored residual size.

\subsection{Model assumptions and score semantics}

Random rotation can spread coordinate energy, motivating a shared
Gaussian-inspired scalar model. It does not force an arbitrary realised
database to have independent, zero-mean Gaussian coordinates. For a fixed
rotation and empirical database mean $\mu$, the transformed mean is
$\Pi\mu$ and $\|\Pi\mu\|=\|\mu\|$. Averaging over random rotations is
different from centring one fixed corpus. Even a uniformly random point on
a sphere has dependent coordinates through its fixed norm. Consequently,
isometry is an algebraic guarantee; the distributional approximation is a
modelling assumption. Chapter 8's centred-coding pilot examines one practical
consequence of that distinction.

The inherited primary levels are Gaussian mid-quantiles. For $X\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2)$ and a zero threshold,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 a_{\rm MSE}
 &=\arg\min_a\mathbb E[(X-a)^2\mid X>0]\\
 &=\mathbb E[X\mid X>0]
 =\sigma\sqrt{2/\pi}\simeq0.79788\sigma.
 \end{aligned}
\] For fixed signs and positive scale, however,
\begin{equation}
 \primarydist=\|q'\|^2+da^2-2a\langle q',s\rangle,
 \qquad s\in\{-1,+1\}^d.
 \label{eq:2-sign-order}
\end{equation}
For fixed signs,
\[
 a>0\Longrightarrow
 \arg\min_x\primarydist(q,x)
 =\arg\max_x\langle q',s(x)\rangle.
\]
Residuals still depend on scale; separability alone gives no optimality.

The scores use different vectors:
\[
 \rawdist=\|q-x\|^2,\qquad
 \primarydist=\|q'-\widehat p\|^2.
\]
\begin{equation}
 \refineddist=\|q'-\widehat p-\widehat r\|^2+\|q'\|^2.
 \label{eq:2-refined}
\end{equation}
Thus, for a fixed query,
\[
 \arg\min_x\refineddist=\arg\min_x\|q'-\widehat p-\widehat r\|^2,
\]
while raw-vector recall remains empirical.

\subsection{Rotation and hierarchical codes}

JHQ first applies a square orthogonal transform
$\Pi\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ to both database vectors and queries
\cite{jhq}. Write $y=\Pi x$ and $q'=\Pi q$. In real arithmetic,
\begin{equation}
 \begin{aligned}
 \Pi^\top\Pi=I
 &\Longrightarrow
 \|\Pi(q-x)\|^2\\
 &=(q-x)^\top\Pi^\top\Pi(q-x)=\|q-x\|^2.
 \end{aligned}
 \label{eq:2-isometry}
\end{equation}
Thus rotation preserves dimension and distances before quantisation.
Finite-precision matrix multiplication is evaluated separately in Chapter 4.

The primary code gives a coarse reconstruction $\widehat p(x)$ of $y$.
In the evaluated configuration, each eight-coordinate subspace uses one
byte: each coordinate takes one of two levels, $-a$ or $+a$, so the byte
records eight signs. More generally, $M$ subspaces have dimension
$D_s=d/M$, with $B$ bits selecting one of $K=2^B$ combinations of
$L=2^{B/D_s}$ scalar levels. For supported parameters with integer $L$,
JHQ uses the Cartesian product
\begin{equation}
 a_i=\sigma\Phi^{-1}\!\left(\frac{i-1/2}{L}\right),\quad
 i=1,\ldots,L,\qquad
 \mathcal C_m=\{a_1,\ldots,a_L\}^{D_s}.
 \label{eq:2-cartesian}
\end{equation}
Here $\Phi$ is the standard normal cumulative distribution function and
$\sigma$ is a scale estimated from vector energy. At $B=D_s=8$, this
gives $L=2$, $\mathcal C_m=\{-a,+a\}^8$ and
$a\simeq0.67449\sigma$. Unit-normalised inputs motivate a scale near
$1/\sqrt d$. The transform and hierarchical representation are inherited
from JHQ.

Residual coding approximates the remaining error,
$r=y-\widehat p$, by $\widehat r$, giving
$\widehat y=\widehat p+\widehat r$. The evaluated residual quantiser learns
scalar levels shared across coordinates within each subspace and uses one
byte per coordinate. Each vector therefore stores $d/8$ primary bytes
and $d$ residual bytes before metadata. A smaller refinement budget reduces
residual reads, while these stored codes remain unchanged.

This residual is relative to the primary reconstruction. By contrast,
residual-coded IVF-PQ subtracts the centroid $\mu_{\ell(x)}$ of the list
containing $x$:
\[
 r_{\rm IVF\text{-}PQ}=x-\mu_{\ell(x)},\qquad
 r_{\rm JHQ}=\Pi x-\widehat p(x).
\]
JHQ uses IVF for routing; its reconstructed vector does not add an IVF centroid.

\subsection{Primary and refined scoring}

Primary screening compares $q'$ with the coarse reconstruction:
\[
 \primarydist=\|q'-\widehat p\|^2.
\]
Only shortlisted candidates are rescored with both primary and residual
codes. The implemented refined score is
\begin{equation}
 \refineddist=\|q'-\widehat p-\widehat r\|^2+\|q'\|^2.
 \label{eq:2-refined}
\end{equation}
The extra term $\|q'\|^2$ is constant across candidates for one query,
so the score orders reconstructed vectors by squared distance. It need
not reproduce the raw-vector ordering used for GT. The score expansion
appears in \cref{eq:5-refined-constant}.

\par\medskip\noindent\begin{minipage}{\linewidth}
\centering\captionsetup{hypcap=false}
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{\input{figures/ch2/candidate-cascade}}
\captionof{figure}[Candidate and scoring cascade]{Candidate and scoring cascade in JHQ.
IVF selects lists, primary scores form a shortlist, and residual codes
refine that shortlist before the final top-$k$ selection.}
\label{fig:2-cascade}
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

With $n_c$ routed vectors, $M$ primary subspaces and up to $c$ survivors,
the score work is
\[
 W_{\rm primary}=O(n_cM)\ \text{lookups},\qquad
 W_{\rm refine}=O(cd)\ \text{coordinates}.
\]
Memory access and candidate selection also contribute to search time.

\subsection{Modelling assumptions}

Random rotation can spread coordinate energy, motivating the Gaussian-inspired
levels above. Distance preservation does not imply independent, zero-mean
Gaussian coordinates: a fixed transform maps a database mean $\mu$ to
$\Pi\mu$, with $\|\Pi\mu\|=\|\mu\|$. Chapter 8 examines centring as an
alternative coding choice.

The primary level is a Gaussian mid-quantile, rather than the level that
minimises reconstruction mean-squared error (MSE). For
$X\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2)$ and a zero decision threshold, the latter is
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 a_{\rm MSE}
 &=\arg\min_a\mathbb E[(X-a)^2\mid X>0]\\
 &=\mathbb E[X\mid X>0]
 =\sigma\sqrt{2/\pi}\simeq0.79788\sigma.
 \end{aligned}
\]
These values serve different objectives. For fixed sign codes, any
positive common primary scale preserves primary ranking
(\cref{eq:4-sign-ranking}); residual reconstruction still depends on the
scale. Thus the algebraic scoring properties do not establish optimal
quantisation or raw-vector recall.

\[
 U(q)=\bigcup_{\ell\in\mathcal L(q)}\mathrm{list}_\ell,\qquad n_c=|U(q)|.
\]
A neighbour outside $U$ cannot be recovered by later scoring.

PQ learns codebooks by subspace \cite{pq}. With unquantised $q$, ADC uses
\begin{equation}
 \|q-\widehat x\|^2=\sum_{m=0}^{M-1}\|q_m-\mathcal C_m[z_m]\|^2.
 \label{eq:2-adc}
\end{equation}
Lookups replace coordinate scoring. A learned subcodebook need not itself be Cartesian; Chapter 5 relies on that extra structure.

The residual definitions differ:
\[
 r_{\rm IVF\text{-}PQ}=x-\mu_{\ell(x)},\qquad
 r_{\rm JHQ}=\Pi x-\widehat p(x).
\]
JHQ therefore adds no IVF centroid during reconstruction. Candidate expansion/refinement is established \cite{johnson_gpu,faiss_refine}.

\begin{equation}
 \mathcal R_\alpha(q)\subseteq C_\alpha(q)\subseteq U(q)\subseteq\mathcal X.
 \label{eq:2-cascade}
\end{equation}
For GT set $\mathcal T_k$, set inclusion gives
\[
 |\mathcal R_\alpha\cap\mathcal T_k|
 \leq |C_\alpha\cap\mathcal T_k|

changes.after:
An inverted-file (IVF) index partitions the database into lists, usually
by assigning each vector to a nearby centroid. A query searches
$n_{\rm probe}$ selected lists. If $\mathcal L(q)$ is their index set,
the vectors available for scoring are
\[
 U(q)=\bigcup_{\ell\in\mathcal L(q)}\mathrm{list}_\ell,\qquad n_c=|U(q)|.
\]
Any true neighbour outside $U(q)$ is excluded before vector scoring begins.

Product quantisation (PQ) compresses each vector by dividing its coordinates
into $M$ subspaces and learning a codebook for each \cite{pq}. In subspace
$m$, the code $z_m$ identifies the representative vector
$\mathcal C_m[z_m]$; together these representatives reconstruct
$\widehat x$. Asymmetric distance computation (ADC) keeps the query
unquantised and evaluates
\begin{equation}
 \|q-\widehat x\|^2=\sum_{m=0}^{M-1}\|q_m-\mathcal C_m[z_m]\|^2.
 \label{eq:2-adc}
\end{equation}
Here $q_m$ is the query's subvector. Distances to codewords are tabulated
once per query, so scanning database codes uses lookups. PQ separates
subspaces, but an arbitrary learned codebook need not separate coordinates
\emph{within} a subspace. JHQ's primary codebook has this additional structure.

Refinement spends more work on a shortlist selected by an initial score
\cite{johnson_gpu,faiss_refine}. Let $\alpha$ be the refinement multiplier
and $c=\max\{k,\lceil\alpha k\rceil\}$ the requested shortlist size.
For $|U(q)|\geq k$, write $C_\alpha(q)$ for up to $c$ retained candidates
and $\mathcal R_\alpha(q)$ for the final $k$ returned vectors. Then
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal R_\alpha(q)\subseteq C_\alpha(q)\subseteq U(q)\subseteq\mathcal X.
 \label{eq:2-cascade}
\end{equation}
If $\mathcal T_k$ is the GT set for the query, inclusion gives
\[
 |\mathcal R_\alpha\cap\mathcal T_k|
 \leq |C_\alpha\cap\mathcal T_k|
 \leq |U\cap\mathcal T_k|.
\]
Increasing probes expands the routed pool; increasing $\alpha$ expands
the requested shortlist. To attribute recall loss to routing, shortlisting
or reconstruction, each stage must be compared while holding the others
fixed. The next section defines JHQ's two scoring stages.

operations \cite{fastscan,quickeradc}. Table size and hardware lookup support are therefore central to speed.

early termination predicts when to stop \cite{li_termination}; DARTH
expresses search effort through recall targets \cite{darth}.

calibration in Chapter 6.

GPU port can overlook. Each eight-bit subspace code indexes 256 distances.

Moving JHQ to a GPU raises three technical challenges.

First, compressed codes reduce storage but can still be expensive to scan.
Each eight-bit primary code addresses a 256-entry distance lookup table
(LUT); these tables must be built and may be too large for fast on-chip memory.
Because JHQ combines per-coordinate quantisation levels, this table can
be split exactly in real arithmetic into two 16-entry tables, one for
each four-bit half of the byte. The challenge is whether the smaller
tables repay the extra lookups and additions on the GPU.

Second, small batches can contain too few queries to keep the GPU busy.
Splitting each query's candidates across thread blocks creates parallel
work, but equal local quotas can discard global winners if the best
candidates fall in one block. One solution is to let each group retain
its own full shortlist before merging, at the cost of memory and merging
work. The challenge
is to retain all potential winners while keeping this overhead below
the parallelism gain. This thesis studies shared cutoffs and batch-dependent
scheduling as ways to reduce that overhead.

Third, the refinement work needed for a target recall varies by workload.
Too few candidates can discard true neighbours; too many spend time
reading and scoring residual codes without improving the answers.
The aim is to choose a reusable budget without ground-truth labels.
A larger-budget search provides a reference, but can itself miss true
neighbours. Agreement with it therefore needs separate checks of recall
on test queries, alongside the cost of calibration and subsequent search.

parallelism can accelerate distance calculations, but raw high-dimensional
vectors can exceed device memory. Compression makes larger indexes
resident; its benefit then depends on how codes are read, candidates are

operations correct and measuring the resulting quality--speed trade-off.

Vector search returns nearby embeddings from a large database. GPU
parallelism can accelerate distance calculations, but raw high-dimensional
vectors can exceed device memory. Compression can make larger indexes
resident, but search still has to read codes and select promising vectors.
JHQ is a hierarchical quantisation method that first compares compact
primary codes to form a shortlist, then uses residual codes for a more
detailed comparison \cite{jhq}. This thesis studies how to execute these
stages efficiently on a GPU while respecting their scoring and selection
rules, and measures the resulting quality--speed trade-off.

Graph-based GPU indexes store vectors and graph links; inverted-file
(IVF) indexes store the representations searched within selected database
partitions \cite{cagra,johnson_gpu,ivfrabitq}. If these structures exceed
device memory, the complete index cannot remain resident.
Our largest benchmark, Stella, contains 17.78 million 1,024-dimensional
text embeddings. Its raw FP32 storage, available device memory and
JHQ-GPU resident allocation, respectively, illustrate the capacity
constraint (\cref{sec:7-7}):
\[
 S_{\rm raw}=67.81\,\mathrm{GiB}
 >S_{\rm GPU}\simeq31.8\,\mathrm{GiB}
 >S_{\rm resident}=20.44\,\mathrm{GiB}.
\]
This motivates a GPU-resident index that searches compressed codes
instead of keeping the full FP32 database on the device.

\subsection{Transform and sampling}

Host QR of a seeded Gaussian matrix produces square $\Pi$:
\begin{equation}
 Y_t=X_t\Pi^{\mathsf T},\qquad y=\Pi x,\qquad
 \|\Pi(q-x)\|_2^2=\|q-x\|_2^2
 \quad\text{when }\Pi^{\mathsf T}\Pi=I.
 \label{eq:4-transform}
\end{equation}
C0 checks finite-precision QR/GEMM error; dimension remains $d$ (\cref{sec:4-6}).

Strided primary/IVF training takes $n_t=39n_{\rm list}$:
\[
 n_t=\begin{cases}159{,}744,&\text{Vogue},\\319{,}488,&\text{arXiv/OpenAI},\\1{,}277{,}952,&\text{BGE/Stella}.\end{cases}
\]
This is Faiss's warning threshold, not a quality guarantee \cite{faiss_clustering}. Residual fitting uses 100,000 rows.

An older twelve-cell Vogue/OpenAI-3072 sweep ($B_r=4/8$, probes 32/128/256) fixed primary/IVF models. With 25 Lloyd iterations, 100K rather than all rows lost at most 0.0018 recall (eleven losses/one tie). Intermediate sizes were non-monotone; this supports bounded training only within that protocol.

\subsection{Why retain the analytical primary model?}

Sample scale and Cartesian levels are
\begin{equation}
 \sigma^2=\frac{1}{n_t d}\sum_{i=0}^{n_t-1}\|x_i\|_2^2,
 \qquad D_s=d/M,\qquad K=2^B.
 \label{eq:4-scale}
\end{equation}
\[
 B=D_s=8\Longrightarrow
 \mathcal C_m=\{-a,+a\}^{8},\quad a=0.674\sigma.
\]
Eight signs fit a byte, enabling $O(d)$ encoding/split LUTs \cite{jhq} (\cref{sec:5-2}). Arbitrary Lloyd updates may break Cartesian structure.

For fixed sign vector $s\in\{-1,+1\}^d$,
\begin{equation}
 \|q'-a s\|^2=\|q'\|^2+da^2-2a\langle q',s\rangle.
 \label{eq:4-sign-ranking}
\end{equation}
\[
 a>0\Longrightarrow
 \arg\min_s\|q'-as\|^2=\arg\max_s\langle q',s\rangle.
\]
The order needs $a>0$, not Gaussian data. Residuals depend on $a$; zero scale/FP32 ties are separate cases.



\subsection{Coarse assignment as filter and refine}

IVF initialises spaced rotated rows and runs eight iterations using $s_\ell=\|\mu_\ell\|^2-2\langle y,\mu_\ell\rangle$. Supported dimensions use int8 filtering, resolving ambiguity in FP32.

\begin{resultblock}
\begin{lemma}[Assignment with certified score intervals]
\label{lem:4-assignment-bound}
Let $\widetilde y,\widetilde\mu_\ell$ be dequantised approximations,
$e=y-\widetilde y$ and $f_\ell=\mu_\ell-\widetilde\mu_\ell$.
Keeping centroid norms exact, the approximate score
$\widetilde s_\ell=\|\mu_\ell\|^2-2\langle\widetilde y,\widetilde\mu_\ell\rangle$
has real-arithmetic error bounded by
\begin{equation}
 E_\ell=2\bigl(\|y\|\|f_\ell\|+\|e\|\|\widetilde\mu_\ell\|\bigr).
 \label{eq:4-assignment-bound}
\end{equation}
Given valid intervals $[L_\ell,U_\ell]$ containing every target score,
discarding only $L_\ell>\min_j U_j$ and exactly resolving the remaining
scores preserves the minimum and its specified tie rule.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Using $e=y-\widetilde y$ and $f_\ell=\mu_\ell-\widetilde\mu_\ell$,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \langle y,\mu_\ell\rangle-
 \langle\widetilde y,\widetilde\mu_\ell\rangle
 &=\langle y,f_\ell\rangle
   +\langle e,\widetilde\mu_\ell\rangle,\\
 |s_\ell-\widetilde s_\ell|
 &\leq2\bigl(\|y\|\|f_\ell\|
       +\|e\|\|\widetilde\mu_\ell\|\bigr)=E_\ell .
 \end{aligned}
\]
For $j^*\in\arg\min_j U_j$,
\[
 L_\ell>U_{j^*}
 \Longrightarrow
 s_\ell\geq L_\ell>U_{j^*}\geq s_{j^*}.
\]
The strict inequality excludes $\ell$; equality stays eligible.
\end{proof}
\end{resultblock}

FP32 headroom lacks a bitwise certificate without accumulation-error bounds. FP16 differs on 0/14,838 Vogue, 6/31,748 BGE and 3/16,359 Stella tail assignments. Cold logs do not identify precision.

\subsection{Residual fitting and the iteration budget}

Residuals stay $r=\Pi x-\widehat p(x)$. Per subspace, GPU sorting/Lloyd fits $K_r=2^{B_r}$ sorted scalar levels shared across coordinates, capped at 2,000 updates.

Historical 100K training gained 0.0063--0.0076 recall at 25$\to$2,000 updates. Tail-bin/BGE/Stella changes persisted: the cap is not convergence, without contradicting exact Lloyd descent. At 20,000 updates, historical Stella all-row/100K recall was 0.9921/0.9920.

\subsection{Construction work and observed imbalance}

\[
 W_{\rm QR}=O(d^3),\qquad W_{\rm rotate}=O(n_t d^2).
\]
Direct coarse assignment costs $O(n_t n_{\rm list}d)$ per iteration.
\[
 W_{\rm primary}=O(MKD_s),\qquad
 W_{\rm residual\ extraction}=O(n_rd),
\]
followed by sorting and scalar updates. These describe work, rather than predict latency.
Synchronised phase diagnostics place about 83\% of BGE/Stella training
in IVF k-means (about 2.97\,s). They use one add buffer and forced
synchronisation, separately from the normal overlapped timings in
\cref{sec:7-7}.


List-size imbalance enters the scan rule in \cref{sec:5-5}. The
individual contributions of eight IVF iterations, spaced seeds and
finite sampling to that imbalance were not isolated.

Sample scale and Cartesian levels are
\begin{equation}

\begin{lemma}[Assignment with certified score intervals]
\label{lem:4-assignment-bound}
Let $\widetilde y,\widetilde\mu_\ell$ be dequantised approximations,
$e=y-\widetilde y$ and $f_\ell=\mu_\ell-\widetilde\mu_\ell$.
Keeping centroid norms exact, the approximate score
$\widetilde s_\ell=\|\mu_\ell\|^2-2\langle\widetilde y,\widetilde\mu_\ell\rangle$
has real-arithmetic error bounded by
\begin{equation}
 E_\ell=2\bigl(\|y\|\|f_\ell\|+\|e\|\|\widetilde\mu_\ell\|\bigr).
 \label{eq:4-assignment-bound}
\end{equation}
Given valid intervals $[L_\ell,U_\ell]$ containing every target score,
discarding only $L_\ell>\min_j U_j$ and exactly resolving the remaining
scores preserves the minimum and its specified tie rule.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Using $e=y-\widetilde y$ and $f_\ell=\mu_\ell-\widetilde\mu_\ell$,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \langle y,\mu_\ell\rangle-
 \langle\widetilde y,\widetilde\mu_\ell\rangle
 &=\langle y,f_\ell\rangle
   +\langle e,\widetilde\mu_\ell\rangle,\\
 |s_\ell-\widetilde s_\ell|
 &\leq2\bigl(\|y\|\|f_\ell\|
       +\|e\|\|\widetilde\mu_\ell\|\bigr)=E_\ell .
 \end{aligned}
\]
For $j^*\in\arg\min_j U_j$,
\[
 L_\ell>U_{j^*}
 \Longrightarrow
 s_\ell\geq L_\ell>U_{j^*}\geq s_{j^*}.
\]
The strict inequality excludes $\ell$; equality stays eligible.
\end{proof}

\frontchapter{Abstract}
Approximate nearest-neighbour (ANN) search supports similarity retrieval
over large collections of embedding vectors. GPUs accelerate this search,
but limited device memory makes compressed indexes attractive. JHQ is a
hierarchical quantisation method that screens candidates with compact
codes and refines a smaller set using residual codes. This thesis develops
JHQ-GPU to study how this representation can support efficient GPU
construction and search.

The implementation combines GPU model fitting and batched encoding with
bounded input staging and a packed, list-ordered layout. Its scan replaces
each 256-entry distance table with two 16-entry tables, preserving scores
in real arithmetic. Grouped scanning preserves exact global candidate
selection under a fixed ordering of computed scores and positions. Calibration chooses how
many candidates to refine without ground-truth labels, by comparing
returned neighbours with a larger-budget reference.

Evaluation on an NVIDIA RTX~5090 compares methods on Vogue, arXiv,
OpenAI-1536 and OpenAI-3072. At recall 0.97 and batch 1,000, JHQ-GPU
delivers $1.32$--$1.75\times$ the host-to-host throughput of CAGRA fp32
across all four datasets and is the fastest tested method on three.
For the larger BGE and Stella datasets, whose raw FP32 vectors exceed
device memory, JHQ-GPU enables single-GPU search; the largest index
contains 17.78 million vectors and uses 20.44\,GiB of resident GPU memory.

changes.after:
倒排文件（IVF）索引将数据库划分为多个列表，通常按向量最近的质心进行分配。查询搜索其中 $n_{\rm probe}$ 个列表。若 $\mathcal L(q)$ 表示选中列表的编号集合，则可参与评分的向量为
\[
 U(q)=\bigcup_{\ell\in\mathcal L(q)}\mathrm{list}_\ell,\qquad n_c=|U(q)|.
\]
位于 $U(q)$ 之外的真实近邻，在向量评分开始之前就已被排除。

乘积量化（product quantisation，PQ）将向量坐标划为 $M$ 个子空间，为每个子空间学习码本，从而压缩向量 \cite{pq}。在子空间 $m$ 中，编码 $z_m$ 指向代表向量 $\mathcal C_m[z_m]$；这些代表向量共同重建 $\widehat x$。非对称距离计算（asymmetric distance computation，ADC）保留未量化的查询，计算
\begin{equation}
 \|q-\widehat x\|^2=\sum_{m=0}^{M-1}\|q_m-\mathcal C_m[z_m]\|^2.
 \label{eq:2-adc}
\end{equation}
其中 $q_m$ 是查询的子向量。每条查询先计算到各码字的距离并制成表，随后扫描数据库编码时使用查表。PQ 分离了不同子空间，但任意学习得到的码本未必能进一步分离同一子空间\emph{内部}的坐标。JHQ 的主码本具有这一额外结构。

精排对初步评分选出的候选短名单投入更多计算 \cite{johnson_gpu,faiss_refine}。令 $\alpha$ 为精排倍率，$c=\max\{k,\lceil\alpha k\rceil\}$ 为请求的短名单大小。在 $|U(q)|\geq k$ 时，以 $C_\alpha(q)$ 表示至多 $c$ 个保留候选，以 $\mathcal R_\alpha(q)$ 表示最终返回的 $k$ 个向量，则
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal R_\alpha(q)\subseteq C_\alpha(q)\subseteq U(q)\subseteq\mathcal X.
 \label{eq:2-cascade}
\end{equation}
若 $\mathcal T_k$ 为该查询的 GT 集合，由包含关系可得
\[
 |\mathcal R_\alpha\cap\mathcal T_k|
 \leq |C_\alpha\cap\mathcal T_k|
 \leq |U\cap\mathcal T_k|.
\]
增加 probe 数会扩大路由候选池；增加 $\alpha$ 会扩大请求的短名单。要区分路由、粗筛或重构导致的召回损失，需要在保持其他阶段固定的条件下逐项比较。下一节定义 JHQ 的两级评分。

优化乘积量化（optimised product quantisation，OPQ）学习旋转和子码本，以减少重构误差 \cite{opq}。ScaNN 的各向异性量化则面向内积近似 \cite{scann}。这种区别很重要，因为最小化向量重构误差未必最有利于保持近邻排序。

RaBitQ 用随机二进制编码估计距离 \cite{rabitq}，其多位扩展提供更细致的表示 \cite{rabitq_multi}。GPU IVF-RaBitQ 将压缩距离估计、IVF 路由与融合搜索结合 \cite{ivfrabitq}。原始单比特 RaBitQ 与本文评测的 JHQ 主码均存储旋转后的符号。JHQ 使用固定重构等级及残差码精排；IVF-RaBitQ 基线测试每维 4/8/9 位的配置。\Cref{sec:7-2,sec:7-smallbatch} 比较完整系统的召回率与吞吐权衡。

Fast Scan 与 Quicker ADC 使用通过单指令多数据（single-instruction, multiple-data，SIMD）操作访问的小表，加速 CPU 距离计算 \cite{fastscan,quickeradc}。因此，表大小与硬件查表支持对速度至关重要。JHQ-GPU 利用主码本内部的坐标结构拆表；第 5 章分析恒等式与有限精度影响。

Faiss 和 GPU 搜索库 cuVS 提供控制精排候选数的参数 \cite{faiss_refine,cuvs_refinement}。Faiss 自动调参使用带标签的评估 \cite{faiss_autotune}；学习式提前终止预测何时停止 \cite{li_termination}；DARTH 用召回目标表达搜索工作量 \cite{darth}。这些方法为第 6 章的无标签校准提供比较依据。

将 JHQ 移植到 GPU 会遇到三个技术挑战。

第一，压缩编码减少了存储，但扫描编码仍可能代价较高。每个八位主码索引一张 256 项的距离查找表（lookup table，LUT）；这些表需要构造，且可能无法放入快速的片上内存。由于 JHQ 通过组合各坐标的量化等级形成编码，这张表可以在实数运算下精确拆成两张 16 项表，分别对应一个字节的前、后四位。挑战在于：更小的表能否抵消额外查表和加法的开销。

第二，小批量可能只有少量查询，不足以充分利用 GPU。将每条查询的候选分给多个线程块可以增加并行工作，但如果各块仅保留相同份额，最好的候选又集中在一个块中，就可能丢失全局优胜者。一种办法是在归并前，让每组各自保留完整的候选短名单，代价是增加显存和归并开销。挑战在于保留所有可能胜出的候选，同时让这些开销低于并行带来的收益。本文研究共享截断阈值和随批量变化的调度，以降低这些开销。

第三，达到目标召回率所需的精排工作量随工作负载变化。候选过少可能丢失真实近邻，过多则可能花时间读取和计算残差编码，却不改善答案。目标是在不使用真值标签的情况下选择可复用预算。较大预算搜索可以提供参考，但它自身也可能漏掉真实近邻。因此，既要在独立测试查询上核查召回率，也要测量校准和后续搜索的成本。

向量检索从大型数据库中返回距离查询较近的嵌入向量。GPU 并行计算可以加速距离计算，但原始高维向量可能超出设备显存。压缩使更大的索引能够常驻 GPU；收益随后取决于编码读取、候选选择和精排的执行方式。本文研究如何将 JHQ 的紧凑层级表示实现为高效 GPU 搜索系统，同时保持这些操作的正确性，并测量质量与速度之间的权衡。

CAGRA 通过图进行导航，压缩 IVF 则扫描选定的倒排列表 \cite{cagra,johnson_gpu,ivfrabitq}。Stella 说明了紧凑存储为何重要（\cref{sec:7-7}）：
\[
 S_{\rm raw}=67.81\,\mathrm{GiB}
 >S_{\rm GPU}=\frac{32607}{1024}\,\mathrm{GiB}
 >S_{\rm resident}=20.44\,\mathrm{GiB}.
\]

JHQ 用主码筛选候选，再以残差对保留下来的候选精排 \cite{jhq}。本文在同一训练索引上改变执行方式和保留候选数，测量召回率、速度、显存和构建成本，也如实报告退步的情况。
changes.after:
向量检索从大型数据库中返回距离查询较近的嵌入向量。GPU 并行计算可以加速距离计算，但原始高维向量可能超出设备显存。压缩可以使更大的索引常驻 GPU，但搜索仍需读取编码并选择有希望的向量。JHQ 是一种层级量化方法，先比较紧凑的主码形成候选短名单，再用残差编码进行更详细的比较 \cite{jhq}。本文研究如何在遵循这些阶段的评分与选择规则的同时，在 GPU 上高效执行它们，并测量质量与速度之间的权衡。

基于图的 GPU 索引存储向量和图连接；倒排文件（inverted file，IVF）索引则存储在选定数据分区中搜索的向量表示 \cite{cagra,johnson_gpu,ivfrabitq}。这些结构若超出设备显存，完整索引便无法常驻。本文最大的基准数据集 Stella 包含 17.78 百万个 1,024 维文本嵌入向量。其原始 FP32 存储需求、设备可用显存和 JHQ-GPU 常驻分配量，依次说明了容量约束（\cref{sec:7-7}）：
\[
 S_{\rm raw}=67.81\,\mathrm{GiB}
 >S_{\rm GPU}\simeq31.8\,\mathrm{GiB}
 >S_{\rm resident}=20.44\,\mathrm{GiB}.
\]
这说明有必要构建常驻 GPU 的压缩索引，直接搜索编码，而非在显存中保存完整的 FP32 数据库。

缓存命中仍需 QR、预热、模型上传和 add。Stella 的 6.67\,s add 包含初始工作区，不含扫描校准／搜索预热，也不是重启时间。

改变 $\alpha$ 无需重训。工作区在图捕获前扩容；改变 batch 大小、保留数、probes、lanes、groups 或 bounds 会触发重新捕获。校准可能绕过捕获。索引拥有的缓冲复用直至释放。

\subsection{Address mapping and four-byte packing}

For list $\ell$, row $r$ maps to
\[
 p=o_\ell+r,\qquad \operatorname{offset}(Z[m,p])=mN+p.
\]
At fixed $m$, $\Delta\operatorname{offset}=\Delta p$. List boundaries can break adjacency.

Pack four subspace bytes per candidate:
\begin{equation}
 \mathsf{w}[j,p]=\sum_{t=0}^{3}2^{8t}Z[4j+t,p],\qquad
 \operatorname{offset}_{\rm bytes}(\mathsf{w}[j,p])=4(jN+p).
 \label{eq:5-packed-layout}
\end{equation}
For $0\leq t<4$ and eight-bit $Z$,
\[
 (\mathsf w[j,p]\gg8t)\mathbin{\&}255=Z[4j+t,p].
\]
Nibbles index \cref{eq:5-lut-factorisation}.

\par\medskip\noindent\begin{minipage}{\linewidth}
\captionsetup{hypcap=false}
\centering
\input{figures/ch5/packed-access}
\captionof{figure}[Packed candidate-parallel access]{Packed candidate-parallel access, showing a subset of warp lanes.
At fixed word group $j$, consecutive positions access adjacent four-byte
words. Each word contains four subspace codes of one candidate. Unpacking
preserves each code byte; LUT splitting happens afterwards. The diagram
illustrates addresses, not a measured number of memory transactions.}
\label{fig:5-packed-access}
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

Construction maps $[M,N]$ bytes to $[M/4,N]$ words ($4\mid M$). Casting would combine candidate bytes. Code-byte costs:
\[
 R=W=NM,\qquad S_{\rm old+new}=2NM.
\]
Repacking is outside search timing.

\subsection{What packed access saves, and what it preserves}

One word load/unpack replaces four byte loads. The logical warp window is $32\times4=128$ bytes; transactions depend on alignment/active lanes. Payload stays $M$ bytes per candidate. Both arms are subspace-major, so transpose/cache effects are not isolated.

changes.after:
This thesis asks how representation-aware execution and workload-level
refinement calibration can make JHQ an efficient, memory-resident GPU ANN
system. Representation-aware execution exploits the code structure in
data layout and scoring; workload-level calibration chooses one reusable
refinement budget from unlabelled queries. Construction and capacity
establish the system's foundation, while cross-system comparisons assess
its practical value. Four research questions follow.

\paragraph{RQ1: GPU index construction and capacity.}
Can a complete JHQ index be built and kept resident on one GPU, and at
what construction time, peak memory and resident capacity (\cref{sec:7-7})?

\paragraph{RQ2: Representation-aware execution.}
How can JHQ's code structure guide GPU table lookup, memory access and
candidate selection to improve throughput while maintaining each stage's
specified ranking and tie rules (\cref{sec:7-3,sec:7-4,sec:7-6})?

\paragraph{RQ3: Workload-level refinement calibration.}
Can a refinement budget calibrated once per workload without ground-truth
labels keep recall on separate test queries close to that of a larger-budget
search and repay its calibration cost (\cref{sec:7-5})?

\paragraph{RQ4: Cross-system search performance.}
Under host-to-host timing, at which recall targets and batch sizes does
JHQ-GPU outperform the tested GPU ANN baselines (\cref{sec:7-2})?

Chapter 3 turns these questions into controlled comparisons. Together they
separate what was built, whether its execution is correct, what effort a
workload requires, and whether the resulting system has useful operating
regions.

CAGRA fp32/int8, IVF-PQ and IVF-RaBitQ \cite{cagra,pq,ivfrabitq}
use separate parameter grids (\cref{tab:3-grids}); FP32 brute force is
exhaustive. Comparisons match recall within these grids, with memory
reported separately, rather than imposing equal storage or tuning cost.

\par\medskip\noindent\begin{minipage}{\linewidth}
\centering\captionsetup{hypcap=false}
\captionof{table}[Principal E1 tuning dimensions]{Principal E1 tuning dimensions. Exact per-point parameters and
coverage extensions remain in the raw records. The grid is finite and
differs between methods.}
\label{tab:3-grids}
\footnotesize\setlength{\tabcolsep}{4pt}
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{.22\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
Family & Recorded search dimensions \\
\midrule
JHQ & Probes and $\alpha$; initial probes 64/128/256 and
$0.5/1/2$ times the workload budget; coverage extensions reach probe
1,024 and larger/smaller budgets \\
CAGRA fp32/int8 & Graph degree 32/64; search width 1/2/4/8;
intermediate top-$k$ capacity 32--512 \\
IVF-PQ & Eight-bit subcodes; 192/384/768-byte codes at $d=768$,
384/768/1,536 at higher dimensions; fp16/fp32 lookup settings;
probes 16--512 \\
IVF-RaBitQ & 4/8/9 bits per dimension, supported search modes,
probes 16--1,024; additional 4,096-list OpenAI indexes \\
GPU brute force & Exhaustive FP32 squared-L2 search, common host boundary \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

The initial JHQ budget anchors are 64, 100, 8 and 4 for
Vogue/arXiv/OpenAI-1536/OpenAI-3072; coverage extensions remain in the
records. For measured points $a,b$, let $R$ be recall and $Q$ throughput.
A point is dominated if another has no lower recall or throughput and
improves at least one:
\[
 a\succ b\iff R_a\geq R_b,\ Q_a\geq Q_b,\
 (R_a,Q_a)\ne(R_b,Q_b).
\]
For target recall $r$, the qualifying measured throughput is
\begin{equation}
Q_{\rm meas}(r)=\max\{Q_i:R_i\geq r\}.
\label{eq:3-measured-frontier}
\end{equation}
Without a qualifying point, this value is undefined. Between adjacent
frontier points bracketing the target, log-throughput interpolation gives
\begin{equation}
\log Q_{\rm int}(r)=(1-\lambda)\log Q_a+\lambda\log Q_b,
\qquad \lambda=\frac{r-R_a}{R_b-R_a}.
\label{eq:3-interpolated-frontier}
\end{equation}
For the interpolated estimate, an absolute recall difference within
$5\times10^{-4}$ selects a measured frontier point directly, taking the
first in increasing-recall order. This can select a point slightly below
the target; it does not relax the measured threshold above. Otherwise
interpolation requires a bracket, and uncovered targets remain unreported.
Small-batch comparisons also retain qualifying measured endpoints.
Near ties report both estimates.

Runs with failed or invalid outputs are excluded from the frontier.
Changes in returned-ID order between repeated calls alone do not
exclude a point (\cref{sec:a-e1-protocol}). CAGRA int8 remains included

DiskANN 将图索引与 SSD 存储结合，搜索超过主存容量的数据库 \cite{diskann}。BANG 借助主机图扩展 GPU 搜索容量 \cite{bang}。这些系统跨越了存储边界，而 JHQ 将压缩层级保持在 GPU 上。因此，本文比较的是常驻执行，而非 SSD 后备搜索。
changes.after:
图索引连接相近向量，沿这些边寻找有希望的候选，而不是扫描选中列表中的全部向量。HNSW 使用分层邻近图进行由粗到细的导航 \cite{hnsw}。在 GPU 上，难点是在遍历过程中提供足够的并行工作。SONG 研究并行图搜索 \cite{song}；CAGRA 面向 GPU 设计图构建与搜索 \cite{cagra}。本文以 CAGRA 作为常驻图索引基线，测试 FP32 和量化向量两种配置。

其他设计通过跨越存储边界扩展容量。DiskANN 将图搜索与 SSD 结合，用于超过主存容量的数据库 \cite{diskann}；BANG 将主机上的图与压缩 GPU 评分结合 \cite{bang}。这些容量增益依赖跨存储边界的通信。

changes.before:
HNSW uses a hierarchy of proximity graphs to guide search from coarse
navigation to finer neighbourhoods \cite{hnsw}. GPU graph search must
also expose enough parallel work during traversal: SONG parallelises
graph search \cite{song}, while CAGRA adjusts connectivity and search
width \cite{cagra}. CAGRA's GPU-resident search makes it the graph
comparator here; both fp32 and quantised configurations are included.

DiskANN combines a graph index with SSD storage to search databases
larger than main memory \cite{diskann}. BANG uses host graphs to extend
GPU search capacity \cite{bang}. These systems move data across a
storage boundary; JHQ instead keeps its compressed hierarchy on the GPU.
The present comparison therefore tests resident execution rather than
SSD-backed search.
changes.after:
Graph indexes connect nearby vectors and navigate these links to find
promising candidates, rather than scanning all vectors in selected lists.
HNSW uses a hierarchy of proximity graphs for coarse-to-fine navigation
\cite{hnsw}. On GPUs, the challenge is to expose parallel work during
traversal. SONG studies parallel graph search \cite{song}; CAGRA designs
graph construction and search for GPUs \cite{cagra}. CAGRA is the resident
graph baseline here, tested with both FP32 and quantised vectors.

Other designs extend capacity across storage boundaries. DiskANN combines
graph search with SSD storage for databases larger than main memory
\cite{diskann}; BANG combines a host-resident graph with compressed GPU
scoring \cite{bang}. Their capacity gains depend on communication across
storage boundaries.

\Cref{tab:3-design} connects each research question to a controlled
comparison. A test configuration, or \emph{cell}, fixes the dataset,
index and workload. Compared variants change the setting under study
while retaining the same trained index, queries, probes, refinement
budget and scoring representation wherever applicable.

the treatment. We summarise $J$ configurations with the geometric mean

changes.before:
This thesis asks how representation-aware execution and workload-level
refinement calibration can make JHQ an efficient, memory-resident GPU ANN
system. Representation-aware execution exploits the code structure in
data layout and scoring; workload-level calibration chooses one reusable
refinement budget from unlabelled queries. Construction and capacity
establish the system's foundation, while cross-system comparisons assess
its practical value. Four research questions follow.

\paragraph{RQ1: GPU index construction and capacity.}
Can a complete JHQ index be built and kept resident on one GPU, and at
what construction time, peak memory and resident capacity (\cref{sec:7-7})?

\paragraph{RQ2: Representation-aware execution.}
How can JHQ's code structure guide GPU table lookup, memory access and
candidate selection to improve throughput while maintaining each stage's
specified ranking and tie rules (\cref{sec:7-3,sec:7-4,sec:7-6})?

\paragraph{RQ3: Workload-level refinement calibration.}
Can a refinement budget calibrated once per workload without ground-truth
labels keep recall on separate test queries close to that of a larger-budget
search and repay its calibration cost (\cref{sec:7-5})?

\paragraph{RQ4: Cross-system search performance.}
Under host-to-host timing, at which recall targets and batch sizes does
JHQ-GPU outperform the tested GPU ANN baselines (\cref{sec:7-2})?

Chapter 3 turns these questions into controlled comparisons. Together they
separate what was built, whether its execution is correct, what effort a
workload requires, and whether the resulting system has useful operating
regions.

\Cref{tab:3-design} connects each research question to a controlled
comparison. A test configuration, or \emph{cell}, fixes the dataset,
index and workload. Compared variants change the setting under study
while retaining the same trained index, queries, probes, refinement
budget and scoring representation wherever applicable.
Let $Q$ denote throughput in queries per second (QPS). A paired speed
ratio is $Q_{\rm treatment}/Q_{\rm control}$; values above one favour
the treatment. We summarise $J$ configurations with the geometric mean
of these ratios, weighting each configuration equally:
\[
 G=\exp\!\left(\frac1J\sum_{j=1}^{J}
 \log\frac{Q_{{\rm treatment},j}}{Q_{{\rm control},j}}\right).
\]

terminology_followup.scope: Clarify undefined terms, compressed sentences and previously unexplained formula parameters; preserve formal mathematics, tables, citations and measured values.

changes.before:
GPU work is organised into thread blocks; threads within a block can
cooperate through shared memory. A warp is a group of 32 threads scheduled
together. Registers, shared memory and limits on resident blocks constrain
how much work can run concurrently \cite{cuda_programming_guide}.
Within this hierarchy, threads can process separate queries, score
different candidates for the same query, or share the coordinate
calculations for one candidate.

Candidate selection keeps the smallest scores from the scanned pool.
Faiss uses warp-level selection \cite{johnson_gpu}; other GPU top-$k$
methods distribute selection over larger arrays \cite{gpu_topk}.
Chapter 5 explains the selection and scheduling used by JHQ-GPU.
changes.after:
GPU work is organised into thread blocks; threads within a block can
cooperate through shared memory. A warp is a group of 32 threads scheduled
together. Blocks run on streaming multiprocessors (SMs). Registers, shared memory
and block limits constrain concurrent work \cite{cuda_programming_guide}.
Occupancy is the fraction of an SM's supported warps that are active.
Nearby addresses accessed by a warp can share memory transactions
(coalesced access); large per-block tables can reduce concurrent work.
Within this hierarchy, threads can process separate queries, score
different candidates for the same query, or share the coordinate
calculations for one candidate.

Candidate selection keeps the smallest scores from the scanned pool.
Faiss uses warp-level selection \cite{johnson_gpu}; other GPU top-$k$
methods distribute selection over larger arrays \cite{gpu_topk}.
Chapter 5 explains the selection and scheduling used by JHQ-GPU.

changes.before:
GPU 工作组织为线程块；块内线程可通过共享内存协作。warp 是一起调度的 32 个线程。寄存器、共享内存以及常驻线程块数量的限制，共同约束可并发执行的工作量 \cite{cuda_programming_guide}。在这一组织方式下，线程可以分别处理不同查询、为同一查询的不同候选评分，或共同计算一个候选的不同坐标。

候选选择从扫描池中保留最小分数。Faiss 使用 warp 级选择 \cite{johnson_gpu}；其他 GPU top-$k$ 方法将选择工作分布到更大的数组上 \cite{gpu_topk}。第 5 章解释 JHQ-GPU 使用的选择与调度方法。

The measured interval is the synchronous host search call:
\[
 t_{\rm call}=t_{\rm return}-t_{\rm entry},
 \quad
 \begin{cases}
 \text{entry: FP32 queries in host memory},\\
 \text{return: host IDs/scores after stream completion}.
 \end{cases}
\]
Staging, transfers, query computation and int8 query quantisation are
included; fitting and construction are excluded (\cref{fig:3-boundary}).
Handles and output buffers are reused.

\par\medskip\noindent\begin{minipage}{\linewidth}
\centering\captionsetup{hypcap=false}
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{\input{figures/ch3/measurement-boundary}}
\captionof{figure}[Host and device timing boundaries]{Timing boundaries. The host interval includes transfers and
query-specific computation. Device-stage profiles explain parts of that
interval; separate profiling and synchronisation can change execution, so
their sum is not an interchangeable end-to-end latency.}
\label{fig:3-boundary}
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

Queries upload through pinned staging buffers. Output buffers are
pageable for JHQ and pinned for the baselines. Harnesses use C++ for
JHQ/RaBitQ and Python for CAGRA/IVF-PQ. Interface costs are included
and matter for small batches and near ties.

For batch size $b$, round $r$ contains $m_r$ calls with durations $t_{ri}$
in seconds. Throughput uses the mean call time within each round, then
the median round throughput:
\begin{equation}
 \bar t_r=\frac1{m_r}\sum_{i=1}^{m_r}t_{ri},
 \qquad Q_r=\frac b{\bar t_r},
 \qquad Q=\operatorname{median}_r Q_r.
 \label{eq:3-throughput}
\end{equation}
E1 uses batches of 1,000 and five rounds, normally with 24 calls each.
JHQ warms once per variant/round; baselines warm three times initially
and reduce call counts for slow configurations. JIT compilation and CUDA
Graph capture precede timing. Call percentiles describe synchronous
batches, rather than concurrent-request tail latency.

Valid slow calls remain in the mean. For illustrative times $(1,1,10)$\,ms,
\[
 \bar t=4\,\mathrm{ms}\ne\operatorname{median}(t)=1\,\mathrm{ms},
 \qquad b/\bar t\ne b/\operatorname{median}(t).
\]
Repeated timing rounds share an index; independent training variation
requires separate cold builds.

E1 used an RTX 5090 with 32,607\,MiB, driver 595.71.05, CUDA 13.0,
cuVS 26.08.01 and a 575\,W power limit. OpenMP used 16 threads with
25 logical CPUs available. JHQ supplied compute\_80 PTX for driver
compilation \cite{cuda_platform}; clocks and host load were not fixed.

Memory reporting distinguishes index allocation, search-time process
allocation and construction peak. Gross process use includes context
and workspace; JHQ's net figure subtracts a background allocation,
whereas CAGRA's index delta measures index allocation
(\cref{sec:4-4,sec:7-7}). These are different accounting boundaries.
Build peaks are sampled every 20\,ms and may miss shorter transients;
construction times cover train/add calls, excluding input loading.

Supplementary campaigns use separate sessions. Cache and arithmetic
conditions are identified in \cref{sec:a-supplement,sec:4-2,sec:7-precision}.

\subsection{Transform and sampling}

Host QR factorisation of a seeded Gaussian matrix produces square $\Pi$:
\begin{equation}
 Y_t=X_t\Pi^{\mathsf T},\qquad y=\Pi x,\qquad
 \|\Pi(q-x)\|_2^2=\|q-x\|_2^2
 \quad\text{when }\Pi^{\mathsf T}\Pi=I.
 \label{eq:4-transform}
\end{equation}
The geometry contract (K0) checks finite-precision QR/GEMM error;
dimension remains $d$ (\cref{sec:4-6}).

Strided primary/IVF training takes $n_t=39n_{\rm list}$:
\[
 n_t=\begin{cases}159{,}744,&\text{Vogue},\\319{,}488,&\text{arXiv/OpenAI},\\1{,}277{,}952,&\text{BGE/Stella}.\end{cases}
\]
This is Faiss's warning threshold, not a quality guarantee \cite{faiss_clustering}. Residual fitting uses 100,000 rows.

An older twelve-cell Vogue/OpenAI-3072 sweep ($B_r=4/8$, probes 32/128/256) fixed primary/IVF models. With 25 Lloyd iterations, 100K rather than all rows lost at most 0.0018 recall (eleven losses/one tie). Intermediate sizes were non-monotone; this supports bounded training only within that protocol.

\subsection{Analytical primary codebook}

Sample scale and Cartesian levels are
\begin{equation}
 \sigma^2=\frac{1}{n_t d}\sum_{i=0}^{n_t-1}\|x_i\|_2^2,
 \qquad D_s=d/M,\qquad K=2^B.
 \label{eq:4-scale}
\end{equation}
\[
 B=D_s=8\Longrightarrow
 \mathcal C_m=\{-a,+a\}^{8},\quad a=0.674\sigma.
\]
Eight signs fit a byte, enabling $O(d)$ encoding/split LUTs \cite{jhq} (\cref{sec:5-2}). Arbitrary Lloyd updates may break Cartesian structure.

For fixed sign vector $s\in\{-1,+1\}^d$,
\begin{equation}
 \|q'-a s\|^2=\|q'\|^2+da^2-2a\langle q',s\rangle.
 \label{eq:4-sign-ranking}
\end{equation}
\[
 a>0\Longrightarrow
 \arg\min_s\|q'-as\|^2=\arg\max_s\langle q',s\rangle.
\]
The order needs $a>0$, not Gaussian data. Residuals depend on $a$; zero scale/FP32 ties are separate cases.



\subsection{Coarse assignment as filter and refine}

IVF initialises spaced rotated rows and runs eight iterations using $s_\ell=\|\mu_\ell\|^2-2\langle y,\mu_\ell\rangle$. Supported dimensions use int8 filtering, resolving ambiguity in FP32.

\begin{resultblock}
\begin{lemma}[Assignment with certified score intervals]
\label{lem:4-assignment-bound}
Let $\widetilde y,\widetilde\mu_\ell$ be dequantised approximations,
$e=y-\widetilde y$ and $f_\ell=\mu_\ell-\widetilde\mu_\ell$.
Keeping centroid norms exact, the approximate score
$\widetilde s_\ell=\|\mu_\ell\|^2-2\langle\widetilde y,\widetilde\mu_\ell\rangle$
has real-arithmetic error bounded by
\begin{equation}
 E_\ell=2\bigl(\|y\|\|f_\ell\|+\|e\|\|\widetilde\mu_\ell\|\bigr).
 \label{eq:4-assignment-bound}
\end{equation}
Given valid intervals $[L_\ell,U_\ell]$ containing every target score,
discarding only $L_\ell>\min_j U_j$ and exactly resolving the remaining
scores preserves the minimum and its specified tie rule.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Using $e=y-\widetilde y$ and $f_\ell=\mu_\ell-\widetilde\mu_\ell$,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \langle y,\mu_\ell\rangle-
 \langle\widetilde y,\widetilde\mu_\ell\rangle
 &=\langle y,f_\ell\rangle
   +\langle e,\widetilde\mu_\ell\rangle,\\
 |s_\ell-\widetilde s_\ell|
 &\leq2\bigl(\|y\|\|f_\ell\|
       +\|e\|\|\widetilde\mu_\ell\|\bigr)=E_\ell .
 \end{aligned}
\]
For $j^*\in\arg\min_j U_j$,
\[
 L_\ell>U_{j^*}
 \Longrightarrow
 s_\ell\geq L_\ell>U_{j^*}\geq s_{j^*}.
\]
The strict inequality excludes $\ell$; equality stays eligible.
\end{proof}
\end{resultblock}

FP32 headroom lacks a bitwise certificate without accumulation-error bounds. FP16 differs on 0/14,838 Vogue, 6/31,748 BGE and 3/16,359 Stella tail assignments. Cold logs do not identify precision.

\subsection{Residual fitting and the iteration budget}

Residuals stay $r=\Pi x-\widehat p(x)$. Per subspace, GPU sorting/Lloyd fits $K_r=2^{B_r}$ sorted scalar levels shared across coordinates, capped at 2,000 updates.

Historical 100K training gained 0.0063--0.0076 recall at 25$\to$2,000 updates. Tail-bin/BGE/Stella changes persisted: the cap is not convergence, without contradicting exact Lloyd descent. At 20,000 updates, historical Stella all-row/100K recall was 0.9921/0.9920.

\subsection{Construction work and observed imbalance}

\[
 W_{\rm QR}=O(d^3),\qquad W_{\rm rotate}=O(n_t d^2).
\]
Direct coarse assignment costs $O(n_t n_{\rm list}d)$ per iteration.
\[
 W_{\rm primary}=O(MKD_s),\qquad
 W_{\rm residual\ extraction}=O(n_rd),
\]
followed by sorting and scalar updates. These describe work, rather than predict latency.
Synchronised phase diagnostics place about 83\% of BGE/Stella training
in IVF k-means (about 2.97\,s). They use one add buffer and forced
synchronisation, separately from the normal overlapped timings in
\cref{sec:7-7}.


List-size imbalance enters the scan rule in \cref{sec:5-5}. The
individual contributions of eight IVF iterations, spaced seeds and
finite sampling to that imbalance were not isolated.


\paragraph{Arithmetic used in the measured implementation.}
The evaluated implementation (v69) stores FP32 matrices but enables cuBLAS
TF32 tensor-core math for $d\geq1{,}536$. In its compiled faithful branch,
a null override falls through to the dimension-based default. This affects
training/add/query rotation and centroid GEMMs on both OpenAI datasets;
an environment override cannot disable that branch. Thus FP32 storage does
not imply full FP32 multiplication. The supplementary FP32 variant (v72)
corrects this switch. Its sensitivity experiment reuses the same
TF32-trained cache and changes add/query arithmetic, rather than retraining
the model in FP32 (\cref{sec:7-precision}).

\subsection{From database IDs to list-ordered positions}

An input row has identifier $i\in\{0,\ldots,N-1\}$. Coarse assignment
places its transformed vector in a list according to the computed
centroid scores. The mathematical assignment target is
\begin{equation}
 a(i)=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{0\leq\ell<n_{\rm list}}
       \|\Pi x_i-\mu_\ell\|_2^2.
 \label{eq:4-assignment}
\end{equation}
Its implementation uses the selected numerical assignment path. Encoding
the primary and residual representations does not subtract $\mu_{a(i)}$;
list membership restricts the future search universe independently of
those reconstructions.

The builder sorts assignments together with a sequence of input IDs.
Let $\rho(p)$ be the input ID at sorted physical position $p$ and let
$o_\ell$ be the start of list $\ell$. The completed arrays satisfy
\begin{equation}
 0=o_0\leq o_1\leq\cdots\leq o_{n_{\rm list}}=N,
 \qquad p\in[o_\ell,o_{\ell+1})\Longrightarrow a(\rho(p))=\ell.
 \label{eq:4-offsets}
\end{equation}
Lower-bound searches give offsets, with
\[
 o_\ell=o_{\ell+1}\Longleftrightarrow\text{list }\ell\text{ is empty}.
\]
Positions are stable within a snapshot, not across builds. All arrays use the same $\rho(p)$.

\begin{figure}[!htbp]
\centering
\input{variants/thesis2/figures/physical-layout}
\caption[Physical GPU index layout]{Physical GPU index layout (schematic).
IVF offsets delimit contiguous physical-position ranges. Independent ID,
word-group-major primary, row-major residual and correction arrays share
position $p$. Byte offsets are relative to each allocation; the illustration
implies neither interleaved allocation nor measured memory transactions.}
\label{fig:4-layout}
\end{figure}

IDs map $p\mapsto\rho(p)$. Two-pass add temporarily builds $\rho^{-1}$ for scatter. Primary ties use positions; final ties use database IDs.

\subsection{Exact addresses and representation widths}

For primary byte $Z[m,p]$,
\[
 \operatorname{offset}_{\rm byte}(Z[m,p])=mN+p.
\] Final packing produces
\begin{equation}
 \mathsf w[j,p]=\sum_{t=0}^{3}2^{8t}Z[4j+t,p],\qquad
 \operatorname{addr}_{\rm byte}(\mathsf w[j,p])=4(jN+p).
 \label{eq:4-primary-address}
\end{equation}
Here $j=0,\ldots,M/4-1$. $\text{word-layout build}\Longrightarrow M\bmod4=0$; other $M$ are rejected. A separate byte-layout compilation
retains the byte representation. Each packed array occupies $NM$ bytes,
but repacking temporarily holds both old and new copies, costing $2NM$.
The one-pass builder
temporarily gathers a vector-major $[N,M]$ primary array, transposes it, and
then repacks; each obsolete copy is freed. The two-pass builder scatters
directly into the subspace-major array before the same final repack.
The search-time lane mapping is discussed in \Cref{sec:5-3}.

Residual codes remain row-major, with
$b_r=\lceil dB_r/8\rceil$ bytes per vector. In the eight-bit configuration,
coordinate $t$ of row $p$ is at byte offset $pb_r+t$. In the four-bit
path it is in byte $pb_r+\lfloor t/2\rfloor$, with even coordinates
in the low nibble and odd coordinates in the high nibble. A four-byte
correction per physical row stores
\begin{equation}
 \gamma[ p ]=2\langle\widehat p(x_{\rho(p)}),
                              \widehat r(x_{\rho(p)})\rangle.
 \label{eq:4-correction}
\end{equation}
Its value must move with that row's codes during gathering or scattering.

List-order primary scans fetch residuals only for survivors. Raw FP32 reranking would add $4Nd$ device bytes. Here compressed reconstructions are refined; Chapter 7 measures recall.

bits (high nibble). A four-byte
correction per physical row stores
\begin{equation}

                              \widehat r(x_{\rho(p)})\rangle.
 \label{eq:4-correction}
\end{equation}
Its value must move with that row's codes during gathering or scattering.

List-order primary scans fetch residuals only for survivors. Raw FP32 reranking would add $4Nd$ device bytes. Here compressed reconstructions are refined; Chapter 7 measures recall.

\subsection{Address mapping and four-byte packing}

For list $\ell$, row $r$ maps to
\[
 p=o_\ell+r,\qquad \operatorname{offset}(Z[m,p])=mN+p.
\]
At fixed $m$, $\Delta\operatorname{offset}=\Delta p$. List boundaries can break adjacency.

Pack four subspace bytes per candidate:
\begin{equation}
 \mathsf{w}[j,p]=\sum_{t=0}^{3}2^{8t}Z[4j+t,p],\qquad
 \operatorname{offset}_{\rm bytes}(\mathsf{w}[j,p])=4(jN+p).
 \label{eq:5-packed-layout}
\end{equation}
For $0\leq t<4$ and eight-bit $Z$,
\[
 (\mathsf w[j,p]\gg8t)\mathbin{\&}255=Z[4j+t,p].
\]
Nibbles index \cref{eq:5-lut-factorisation}.

Local top-$c$ can emit $\gscan c$ intermediate entries for $c$ winners. Shared bounds reduce this maintenance. The scheduler
then chooses how much scan parallelism to expose. Both operate at a fixed

\subsection{A complete-key upper bound with explicit witnesses}

Let $K_{(c)}$ be the global $c$th key when $|U|\geq c$. If a group holds
$c$ distinct, fully scored candidates, the largest key among those
witnesses, $\tau_j$, satisfies $K_{(c)}\preceq\tau_j$. There are already
$c$ candidates no later than $\tau_j$ in the global universe. The shared
bound is initialised to a top sentinel and updated by
\begin{equation}
 \tau\leftarrow\min_{\prec}(\tau,\tau_j).
 \label{eq:5-shared-update}
\end{equation}
No bound is published from fewer than $c$ valid candidates. If the entire
universe has fewer than $c$, no group can publish such a bound and all
valid candidates remain eligible.

\begin{resultblock}
\begin{proposition}[Safe rejection by a witnessed bound]
\label{prop:5-shared-bound}
Assume fixed keys, publications backed by $c$ distinct candidates, and
reads that return either the initial sentinel or one complete published
key. Rejecting a candidate only when $K_q(x)\succ\tau$ cannot remove a
global top-$c$ candidate, irrespective of publication timing.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
A publication has a set $W_\tau$ of $c$ distinct witnesses:
\[
 \max_{x\in W_\tau}K_q(x)\preceq\tau
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad K_{(c)}\preceq\tau.
\]
Sentinel reads and minima of published keys obey the same inequality. Thus
\[
 x\in\operatorname{Top}_c(U)
 \ \Longrightarrow\ K_q(x)\preceq K_{(c)}\preceq\tau_{\rm seen}
 \ \Longrightarrow\ x\text{ is not rejected}.
\]
Stale reads only loosen the bound. Publications
made after earlier safe rejections remain valid: any $c$ retained
distinct candidates still supply $c$ witnesses, whether or not they are
the best $c$ of their group.
\end{proof}
\end{resultblock}

Shared filtering retains global coverage (\cref{prop:5-local-coverage}). Admission is
\begin{equation}
 K_q(x)\prec\lambda_j
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 K_q(x)\preceq\tau_{\rm seen},
 \label{eq:5-admission}
\end{equation}
Here $\lambda_j$ is the local compaction threshold and $\tau_{\rm seen}$ the last shared key read. The shared comparison retains equality.

\subsection{Publication, filtering and implementation limits}

For nonnegative FP32 scores, canonical positive zero and valid nonnegative positions,
\begin{equation}
 \kappa(D,p)=2^{32}\operatorname{uintbits}_{32}(D)+p.
 \label{eq:5-packed-key}
\end{equation}
On this non-NaN domain, monotone float bits give
\[
 (D_1,p_1)\prec(D_2,p_2)\iff\kappa(D_1,p_1)<\kappa(D_2,p_2).
\]
Finite keys precede infinity and the all-one sentinel. Invalid positions cannot publish.

\subsection{Choosing parallelism without changing the budget}

$b\gscan$ blocks add parallelism and staging/selection/merge costs. Smaller quotas require a certificate or fallback. Concentrated pilot survivors motivated witnessed bounds (\cref{sec:7-4}).

Define
\[
 T_{\rm blk}=\text{scan threads/block},\quad
 H=n_{\rm SM}T_{\rm resident/SM},\quad
 v=\frac{\operatorname{sd}(n_c)}{\operatorname{mean}(n_c)}.
\] Its rule is
\begin{align}
 g_{\rm fill}
 &=\max\!\left(\{1\}\cup
       \{h\in\{2,4,8\}:bhT_{\rm blk}\leq0.6H\}\right),
       \label{eq:5-fill-rule}\\
 g_{\rm skew}&=
   \begin{cases}4,&v\geq0.3,\\1,&v<0.3,\end{cases}
 \qquad
 g_{\rm chosen}=\max(g_{\rm fill},g_{\rm skew}).
 \label{eq:5-skew-rule}
\end{align}
The skew rule may override the fill limit. In the evaluation harness,
$v$ is calibrated using 512 database vectors as pseudoqueries and a
fixed routing configuration; it uses no ground-truth labels. This is
distinct from Chapter 6's sampled output-agreement calibration. Once
calibrated, scheduling uses the batch size and stored statistic without
an additional per-search host readback. The constants were fitted on
four pilot configurations and then evaluated on further configurations.
The one-time pseudoquery calibration is excluded from
the reported steady-state search times. Observed startup ranges, separate from refinement-budget calibration (\cref{sec:a-supplement}), are
\[
 T_{\rm gather}\in[0.81,7.04]\,\mathrm{ms},\quad
 T_{\rm first}\in[6.00,27.77]\,\mathrm{ms},\quad
 \operatorname{median}(T_{\rm repeat})\in[2.72,18.13]\,\mathrm{ms}.
\]

Choosing one group dispatches $\gscan=0$ at fixed index/probes/budget. Its distance-only ties need a common-order check for identical survivors. Integrated gains/regret are in \cref{sec:7-6}.

\subsection{Observed execution paths}

On the 170-SM RTX 5090 (48 warps/SM) \cite{blackwell_tuning},
\[
 1000\cdot2\cdot512=1{,}024{,}000
 >0.6\cdot170\cdot48\cdot32=156{,}672.
\]
Fill therefore chooses one group; skew can override to four.

In E1, 9/38 records cross $v=0.3$, all Vogue ($0.338$--$0.622$). Its 27 cells use four groups; 105 arXiv/OpenAI cells use $\gscan=0$. Their gains use LUTs, packing, lanes and probe selection, without grouped retention/bounds.

Vogue: 3--15 pure-tie differences/1,000 queries, zero non-tie differences, identical final outputs. At 128 probes the tie range is 7--11.

Observed cell counts are
\[
 \begin{array}{c|rrr}
 &G=0&G=2&G=4\\\hline
 \text{held-out}&10&0&2\\
 S=128&2&8&2
 \end{array}
\]
Eight of twelve switch paths. Benefits depend on load size/skew, without a fixed batch-256 cutoff.

The heuristic omits residency/compaction/merge costs; pseudoqueries can age. Worst measured regret is 1.217 at batch 256. Budgets stay fixed; \cref{sec:5-6} handles refinement.

\begin{equation}

 \label{eq:5-probe-score}
\end{equation}
Omitting the common query norm preserves centroid ordering. In contrast
to primary squared-distance tables, these scores can be negative. The output is
\[
 n_{\rm sel}=\min(n_{\rm probe},n_{\rm list}),\qquad

\subsection{Radix selection followed by deterministic ordering}

One block makes four MSB-first radix passes. For prefix-restricted histogram $H_t$ and one-based residual rank $r_t$ ($r_0=n_{\rm sel}$),
\[
 b_t=\min\Bigl\{b:\sum_{a\leq b}H_t[a]\geq r_t\Bigr\},\qquad
 r_{t+1}=r_t-\sum_{a<b_t}H_t[a].
\]
The chosen bin extends the prefix. Four bytes fix the cutoff/equal-key count.

Canonicalise signed zeros to positive zero, then map bits $u$ by
\begin{equation}
 F(u)=\begin{cases}
       \mathop{\sim}u,&\text{if the sign bit is set},\\
       u\mathbin{|}2^{31},&\text{otherwise}.
      \end{cases}
 \label{eq:5-probe-key}
\end{equation}
For non-NaN scores, monotonicity follows by cases:
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 D_1<D_2<0&\Rightarrow u_1>u_2\Rightarrow{\sim}u_1<{\sim}u_2,\\
 0\leq D_1<D_2&\Rightarrow u_1<u_2\Rightarrow
 (u_1\mathbin{|}2^{31})<(u_2\mathbin{|}2^{31}),\\
 D_1<0\leq D_2&\Rightarrow F(u_1)<2^{31}\leq F(u_2).
 \end{aligned}
\]
Infinities/zeros are covered, unlike the nonnegative-only \cref{eq:5-packed-key}. Repeated \texttt{fma} fixes recomputed keys.

Histogram storage is
\[
 256\ \text{bins}\times32\ \text{lane replicas}\times4\ \text{bytes}=32\,\mathrm{KiB}.
\]
Replication reduces same-warp collisions, leaving inter-warp contention/reduction cost.

Let $h$ be the cutoff key. Collection forms
\[
 A_< =\{i:F(u_i)<h\},\quad A_= =\{i:F(u_i)=h\},\quad
 m=n_{\rm sel}-|A_<|.
\]
Take $A_<$ plus the $m$ smallest IDs in $A_=$, using ordered ballots/prefix counts rather than atomic arrival. For the resulting set $A$,
\[
 \operatorname{rank}(i)=|\{j\in A:(s_j,j)\prec(s_i,i)\}|,
 \qquad\mathrm{out}[\operatorname{rank}(i)]=i.
\]

Selected lengths produce prefix offsets. For excess probes,
\[
 i_j=i_{n_{\rm sel}-1},\quad L_j=0\quad(j\geq n_{\rm sel}),
 \qquad\omega_{j+1}=\omega_j+L_j.
\]
Zero lengths prevent rescans. Require $n_{\rm list},n_{\rm probe}>0$.

Histogram/collection reread scores; ranking is $O(n_{\rm sel}^2)$ with growing shared memory. Small selections still pay fixed histogram storage; this is deterministic integration, not uniform linear cost.

Tests cover ties/zeros/infinities/extremes/excess probes (\cref{sec:7-4}).

FP16 approximation and cross-process checks are separate (\cref{sec:7-4}).

\[
 \frac{T'}T=1+f\left(\frac1s-1\right)>1

\label{sec:8-rank}

FP64 candidate replay uses 400/200/400 calibration/\allowbreak{}validation/\allowbreak{}test queries. Lower MSE can worsen neighbour order; primary-level changes also move residual reference points.

Median thresholds reduce arXiv's minimum tested qualifying count 875$\to$375; two other workloads fail. For orthogonal $\Pi$,
\[

changes.before:
The measured interval is the synchronous host search call:
\[
 t_{\rm call}=t_{\rm return}-t_{\rm entry},
 \quad
 \begin{cases}
 \text{entry: FP32 queries in host memory},\\
 \text{return: host IDs/scores after stream completion}.
 \end{cases}
\]
Staging, transfers, query computation and int8 query quantisation are
included; fitting and construction are excluded (\cref{fig:3-boundary}).
Handles and output buffers are reused.

\par\medskip\noindent\begin{minipage}{\linewidth}
\centering\captionsetup{hypcap=false}
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{\input{figures/ch3/measurement-boundary}}
\captionof{figure}[Host and device timing boundaries]{Timing boundaries. The host interval includes transfers and
query-specific computation. Device-stage profiles explain parts of that
interval; separate profiling and synchronisation can change execution, so
their sum is not an interchangeable end-to-end latency.}
\label{fig:3-boundary}
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

Queries upload through pinned staging buffers: host memory locked against
paging for GPU transfers. JHQ outputs use ordinary pageable host memory;
baseline outputs use pinned memory. Harnesses use C++ for
JHQ/RaBitQ and Python for CAGRA/IVF-PQ. Interface costs are included
and matter for small batches and near ties.

For batch size $b$, round $r$ contains $m_r$ calls with durations $t_{ri}$
in seconds. Throughput uses the mean call time within each round, then
the median round throughput:
\begin{equation}
 \bar t_r=\frac1{m_r}\sum_{i=1}^{m_r}t_{ri},
 \qquad Q_r=\frac b{\bar t_r},
 \qquad Q=\operatorname{median}_r Q_r.
 \label{eq:3-throughput}
\end{equation}
E1 uses batches of 1,000 and five rounds, normally with 24 calls each.
JHQ warms once per variant/round; baselines warm three times initially
and reduce call counts for slow configurations. Driver just-in-time (JIT) compilation and CUDA Graph capture, which
records GPU operations for replay, precede timing. Call percentiles describe synchronous
batches, rather than concurrent-request tail latency.

Valid slow calls remain in the mean. For illustrative times $(1,1,10)$\,ms,
\[
 \bar t=4\,\mathrm{ms}\ne\operatorname{median}(t)=1\,\mathrm{ms},
 \qquad b/\bar t\ne b/\operatorname{median}(t).
\]
Repeated timing rounds share an index; independent training variation
requires separate cold builds.

E1 used an RTX 5090 with 32,607\,MiB, driver 595.71.05, CUDA 13.0,
cuVS 26.08.01 and a 575\,W power limit. OpenMP used 16 threads with
25 logical CPUs available. JHQ supplied compute\_80 PTX, NVIDIA's intermediate GPU instructions,
for driver compilation \cite{cuda_platform}; clocks and host load were not fixed.

Memory reporting distinguishes index allocation, search-time process
allocation and construction peak. Gross process use includes context
and workspace; JHQ's net figure subtracts a background allocation,
whereas CAGRA's index delta measures index allocation
(\cref{sec:4-4,sec:7-7}). These are different accounting boundaries.
Build peaks are sampled every 20\,ms and may miss shorter transients;
construction times cover train/add calls, excluding input loading.

Supplementary campaigns use separate sessions. Cache and arithmetic
conditions are identified in \cref{sec:a-supplement,sec:4-2,sec:7-precision}.

changes.before:
测量区间为同步的主机搜索调用：
\[
 t_{\rm call}=t_{\rm return}-t_{\rm entry},
 \quad
 \begin{cases}
 \text{entry: FP32 queries in host memory},\\
 \text{return: host IDs/scores after stream completion}.
 \end{cases}
\]
计入暂存、传输、查询计算和 int8 查询量化；拟合与构建不计入（\cref{fig:3-boundary}）。句柄和输出缓冲复用。

\par\medskip\noindent\begin{minipage}{\linewidth}
\centering\captionsetup{hypcap=false}
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{\input{figures/ch3/measurement-boundary}}
\captionof{figure}[主机与设备计时边界]{计时边界。主机区间包含传输和查询专属计算。设备阶段剖析解释其中部分时间；独立剖析和同步可能改变执行，因此阶段时间之和不能替代端到端延迟。}
\label{fig:3-boundary}
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

查询通过页锁定（pinned）暂存缓冲上传，即使用不会被操作系统换页的主机内存进行 GPU 传输。JHQ 输出使用普通可换页（pageable）主机内存，基线输出使用页锁定内存。JHQ／RaBitQ 程序使用 C++，CAGRA／IVF-PQ 使用 Python。接口成本计入测量，对小 batch 与接近持平的比较尤其重要。

对大小为 $b$ 的 batch，第 $r$ 轮包含 $m_r$ 次调用，每次耗时 $t_{ri}$，单位为秒。先用轮内平均调用时间计算吞吐，再取各轮吞吐的中位数：
\begin{equation}
 \bar t_r=\frac1{m_r}\sum_{i=1}^{m_r}t_{ri},
 \qquad Q_r=\frac b{\bar t_r},
 \qquad Q=\operatorname{median}_r Q_r.
 \label{eq:3-throughput}
\end{equation}
E1 使用大小为 1,000 的 batch，测量五轮，通常每轮 24 次。JHQ 每个变体／轮次预热一次；基线起初预热三次，并为慢配置减少计时调用数。驱动即时（just-in-time，JIT）编译和 CUDA Graph 捕获均在计时前完成；后者记录 GPU 操作，供后续重复执行。调用时间分位数描述同步 batch，而非并发请求的尾延迟。

有效的慢调用保留在均值中。以示意时间 $(1,1,10)$\,ms 为例，
\[
 \bar t=4\,\mathrm{ms}\ne\operatorname{median}(t)=1\,\mathrm{ms},
 \qquad b/\bar t\ne b/\operatorname{median}(t).
\]
重复计时轮次共享同一索引；独立训练波动需要单独冷建库测量。

E1 使用 RTX 5090，显存 32,607\,MiB，驱动 595.71.05，CUDA 13.0，cuVS 26.08.01，功率上限 575\,W。OpenMP 使用 16 个线程，环境提供 25 个逻辑 CPU。JHQ 提供 compute\_80 PTX（NVIDIA 的 GPU 中间指令），由驱动编译 \cite{cuda_platform}；频率和主机负载未固定。

显存统计区分索引分配、搜索时进程分配与构建峰值。进程总占用包含上下文和工作区；JHQ 的净值扣除背景分配，CAGRA 的索引增量则衡量索引分配（\cref{sec:4-4,sec:7-7}），二者边界不同。构建峰值每 20\,ms 采样，可能遗漏更短的瞬时峰值；构建时间覆盖 train／add 调用，不含输入载入。

补充实验使用独立会话；缓存与算术条件见\cref{sec:a-supplement,sec:4-2,sec:7-precision}。

\subsection{Transform and sampling}

QR factorisation on the host splits a seeded Gaussian matrix into
orthogonal and upper-triangular factors; the orthogonal factor gives
square $\Pi$:
\begin{equation}
 Y_t=X_t\Pi^{\mathsf T},\qquad y=\Pi x,\qquad
 \|\Pi(q-x)\|_2^2=\|q-x\|_2^2
 \quad\text{when }\Pi^{\mathsf T}\Pi=I.
 \label{eq:4-transform}
\end{equation}
The geometry contract (K0) checks rounding in QR and general matrix
multiplication (GEMM);
dimension remains $d$ (\cref{sec:4-6}).

Primary/IVF training selects regularly spaced database rows, requesting
$n_t=39n_{\rm list}$:
\[
 n_t=\begin{cases}159{,}744,&\text{Vogue},\\319{,}488,&\text{arXiv/OpenAI},\\1{,}277{,}952,&\text{BGE/Stella}.\end{cases}
\]
This is Faiss's warning threshold, not a quality guarantee \cite{faiss_clustering}. Residual fitting uses 100,000 rows.

An older twelve-cell Vogue/OpenAI-3072 sweep ($B_r=4/8$, probes 32/128/256) fixed primary/IVF models. With 25 Lloyd iterations, 100K rather than all rows lost at most 0.0018 recall (eleven losses/one tie). Intermediate sizes were non-monotone; this supports bounded training only within that protocol.

\subsection{Analytical primary codebook}

Sample scale and Cartesian levels are
\begin{equation}
 \sigma^2=\frac{1}{n_t d}\sum_{i=0}^{n_t-1}\|x_i\|_2^2,
 \qquad D_s=d/M,\qquad K=2^B.
 \label{eq:4-scale}
\end{equation}
\[
 B=D_s=8\Longrightarrow
 \mathcal C_m=\{-a,+a\}^{8},\quad a=0.674\sigma.
\]
Eight signs fit a byte, enabling $O(d)$ encoding/split LUTs \cite{jhq} (\cref{sec:5-2}). Arbitrary Lloyd updates may break Cartesian structure.

For fixed sign vector $s\in\{-1,+1\}^d$,
\begin{equation}
 \|q'-a s\|^2=\|q'\|^2+da^2-2a\langle q',s\rangle.
 \label{eq:4-sign-ranking}
\end{equation}
\[
 a>0\Longrightarrow
 \arg\min_s\|q'-as\|^2=\arg\max_s\langle q',s\rangle.
\]
The order needs $a>0$, not Gaussian data. Residuals depend on $a$; zero scale/FP32 ties are separate cases.



\subsection{Coarse assignment as filter and refine}

IVF initialises spaced rotated rows and runs eight iterations using $s_\ell=\|\mu_\ell\|^2-2\langle y,\mu_\ell\rangle$. Supported dimensions use int8 filtering, resolving ambiguity in FP32.

\begin{resultblock}
\begin{lemma}[Assignment with certified score intervals]
\label{lem:4-assignment-bound}
Let $\widetilde y,\widetilde\mu_\ell$ be dequantised approximations,
$e=y-\widetilde y$ and $f_\ell=\mu_\ell-\widetilde\mu_\ell$.
Keeping centroid norms exact, the approximate score
$\widetilde s_\ell=\|\mu_\ell\|^2-2\langle\widetilde y,\widetilde\mu_\ell\rangle$
has real-arithmetic error bounded by
\begin{equation}
 E_\ell=2\bigl(\|y\|\|f_\ell\|+\|e\|\|\widetilde\mu_\ell\|\bigr).
 \label{eq:4-assignment-bound}
\end{equation}
Given valid intervals $[L_\ell,U_\ell]$ containing every target score,
discarding only $L_\ell>\min_j U_j$ and exactly resolving the remaining
scores preserves the minimum and its specified tie rule.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Using $e=y-\widetilde y$ and $f_\ell=\mu_\ell-\widetilde\mu_\ell$,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \langle y,\mu_\ell\rangle-
 \langle\widetilde y,\widetilde\mu_\ell\rangle
 &=\langle y,f_\ell\rangle
   +\langle e,\widetilde\mu_\ell\rangle,\\
 |s_\ell-\widetilde s_\ell|
 &\leq2\bigl(\|y\|\|f_\ell\|
       +\|e\|\|\widetilde\mu_\ell\|\bigr)=E_\ell .
 \end{aligned}
\]
For $j^*\in\arg\min_j U_j$,
\[
 L_\ell>U_{j^*}
 \Longrightarrow
 s_\ell\geq L_\ell>U_{j^*}\geq s_{j^*}.
\]
The strict inequality excludes $\ell$; equality stays eligible.
\end{proof}
\end{resultblock}

FP32 headroom lacks a bitwise certificate without accumulation-error bounds. FP16 differs on 0/14,838 Vogue, 6/31,748 BGE and 3/16,359 Stella tail assignments. Cold logs do not identify precision.

\subsection{Residual fitting and the iteration budget}

Residuals stay $r=\Pi x-\widehat p(x)$. Per subspace, GPU sorting/Lloyd fits $K_r=2^{B_r}$ sorted scalar levels shared across coordinates, capped at 2,000 updates.

Historical 100K training gained 0.0063--0.0076 recall at 25$\to$2,000 updates. Tail-bin/BGE/Stella changes persisted: the cap is not convergence, without contradicting exact Lloyd descent. At 20,000 updates, historical Stella all-row/100K recall was 0.9921/0.9920.

\subsection{Construction work and observed imbalance}

\[
 W_{\rm QR}=O(d^3),\qquad W_{\rm rotate}=O(n_t d^2).
\]
Direct coarse assignment costs $O(n_t n_{\rm list}d)$ per iteration.
\[
 W_{\rm primary}=O(MKD_s),\qquad
 W_{\rm residual\ extraction}=O(n_rd),
\]
followed by sorting and scalar updates. These describe work, rather than predict latency.
Synchronised phase diagnostics place about 83\% of BGE/Stella training
in IVF k-means (about 2.97\,s). They use one add buffer and forced
synchronisation, separately from the normal overlapped timings in
\cref{sec:7-7}.


List-size imbalance enters the scan rule in \cref{sec:5-5}. The
individual contributions of eight IVF iterations, spaced seeds and
finite sampling to that imbalance were not isolated.


\paragraph{Arithmetic used in the measured implementation.}
The evaluated implementation (v69) stores FP32 matrices but enables cuBLAS
TF32 tensor-core math for $d\geq1{,}536$. In its compiled faithful branch,
a null override falls through to the dimension-based default. This affects
training/add/query rotation and centroid GEMMs on both OpenAI datasets;
an environment override cannot disable that branch. Thus FP32 storage does
not imply full FP32 multiplication. The supplementary FP32 variant (v72)
corrects this switch. Its sensitivity experiment reuses the same
TF32-trained cache and changes add/query arithmetic, rather than retraining
the model in FP32 (\cref{sec:7-precision}).

multiplication (GEMM);
dimension remains $d$ (\cref{sec:4-6}).
